Introduction to Software Design Patterns

Course References
•
Primary reference: Eric Freeman and Elisabeth Robson, Head First Design Patterns,
2nd ed., O’Reilly Media, 2020.
•
Supplementary reference: Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson, and John
Vlissides, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (GoF).
Chapter 1 • Introduction to Design Patterns

Software Design patterns 
•
Software development problems are often recurring problems.
•
Other developers have already encountered and solved many design problems.
•
Design patterns translate accumulated object-oriented experience into reusable
designs.
•
Patterns provide experience reuse, rather than simply code reuse.
•
Software Design patterns are proven ways to organize software to solve common
design problems; they give us a design solution, not ready-made code.
Chapter 1 • Introduction to Design Patterns

What is Good Software Design?
•
Maintainable: easy to modify when requirements change.
•
Reusable: behaviors or components can be reused in other scenarios.
•
Flexible: new behavior can be added without major restructuring.
•
Extensible: the system can grow without becoming difficult to manage.
•
Knowing OO: OO concepts such as inheritance and polymorphism does not 
automatically produce good design.
Chapter 1 • Introduction to Design Patterns

Why Software Design must Handle Change
•
Change is presented as the constant in software development.
•
Users may request new functionality.
•
Organizations may change vendors, data formats, protocols, or technologies.
•
Good design aims to make changes with the least possible impact on existing code.
Chapter 1 • Introduction to Design Patterns

Maintainability
•
Maintainability is the ability to modify and update software without widespread 
unintended effects.
•
Poor design can cause:

Changes in one class to affect many other classes.

Repeated modifications.

Duplicate code.

Increased chance of bugs.

Difficult maintenance.
Chapter 1 • Introduction to Design Patterns

Example: SimUDuck
•
Joe works for a company that makes a highly successful duck pond simulation game, SimUDuck. 
•
The game can show a wide variety of duck species swimming and making quacking sounds. 
•
The initial designers of the system used standard OO techniques and created a single superclass 
called Duck from which all other duck types inherit.

Chapter 1 • Introduction to Design Patterns

Problems with Inheritance
•
All subclasses inherit behavior from the superclass.
•
Some subclasses may inherit behavior they should not have.
•
Behavior may need to be overridden repeatedly.
•
Different behaviors make inheritance difficult to maintain because each new type may 
need special code or changes.
•
Changes can unintentionally affect other subclasses.
Chapter 1 • Introduction to Design Patterns

Reusability
•
Inheritance can provide reuse, but it can also introduce unwanted behavior.
•
Not every subclass needs every inherited behavior.
•
Better approach: Separating behaviors into independent classes allows them to be 
reused.
•
Example: The same flying behavior can be reused by different classes, not just Ducks.

Chapter 1 • Introduction to Design Patterns

Flexibility
•
A flexible design allows behavior to be changed or extended easily.
•
Behavior implementations can be exchanged through a common interface.
Chapter 1 • Introduction to Design Patterns

Coupling and Cohesion
•
Coupling:
describes
how
strongly
one
class/component
depends
on
other
classes/components.
•
Design goal: reduce unnecessary dependencies so changes remain localized.
•
Cohesion: describes how closely the responsibilities of a class/module belong
together.
•
Design goal: keep related responsibilities together and separate unrelated or
changing responsibilities.
•
Instead of placing all flying and quacking implementations inside Duck, the changing
behaviors are separated into dedicated classes.
Chapter 1 • Introduction to Design Patterns

Encapsulate What Varies
•
Take the parts that vary and “encapsulate” them, so that later you can alter or extend 
the parts that vary without affecting the rest of your code.
•
Benefits: 
•
Fewer unintended consequences from code changes and more flexibility in your 
systems!
•
In SimUDuck, flying and quacking vary across ducks.
•
Move those behaviors into separate behavior classes.
Chapter 1 • Introduction to Design Patterns       
Design Principle: Identify the aspects of your application 
that vary and separate them from what stays the same.
